nodes.label: arch/ versus hal/
nodes.rationale: arch/ is 'which CPU are you' and is reimplemented rather than abstracted; hal/ is 'which peripheral do you have' and does get a common interface, because pushing out a character is pushing out a character. Two boards with the same CPU share arch/ and differ in hal/.

nodes.label: The HAL interface, minimal on purpose
nodes.rationale: Do not expand it speculatively: an abstraction written against a single target is that target's shape with generic names. hal.h is the authority and the listing in the document is a summary.

nodes.label: hal_fb_init
nodes.rationale: Ask the firmware for a linear framebuffer and let it choose where the pixels live - the one operation ramfb and the Pi mailbox both perform.

nodes.label: hal_irq_handle
nodes.source_location: The interrupt controller has to move
nodes.rationale: It takes no argument on purpose: the ARM side reads the GIC's IAR here, so asking the 8259 which line is in service costs two port accesses a tick and keeps arch/x86_64/trap.c from ever learning what a PIC is.

nodes.label: hal_ticks_missed
nodes.source_location: The interrupt controller has to move
nodes.rationale: Returns 0 on the PC and says why: the ARM timer is one-shot so a missed deadline is a comparison the re-arm was making anyway, while the PIT free-runs and the 8259 collapses repeats into one pending bit.

nodes.label: hal_pointer_poll
nodes.rationale: Reports in the device's own units with the range beside them, because only the window manager knows how big the screen is and only it can scale.

nodes.label: The hal_net frame interface
nodes.rationale: Frames and nothing above them: no addresses, no protocols, no checksums. What an IP address means is not a driver's business, and a HAL that grew one would have an opinion about the internet.

nodes.label: hal_fb_flush, the entry virtio-gpu will add
nodes.rationale: virtio-gpu does not fit hal_fb_init's shape - it needs an explicit flush - which is exactly why adding it is what grows the interface, with two implementations in front of it rather than one.

nodes.label: x86-64, the second architecture
nodes.source_location: x86-64, and what a second architecture cost
nodes.rationale: It runs the desktop on QEMU q35 and passes the same 62 display checks in the same time as aarch64. Cost, once kernel/ compiled, was almost entirely device plumbing; with two AArch64 targets the layer boundary is a promise, and with x86-64 it becomes a compile error.

nodes.label: Building long mode
nodes.rationale: ARM hands you 64-bit execution and asks which privilege level; x86 starts in real mode and long mode has to be built - page tables, a GDT with the L bit, CR4.PAE, EFER.LME, CR0.PG and a far jump, in that order. Page tables live in .bss so zeroing must come first; rdmsr answers in EDX:EAX; a multiboot loader parses ELF32, so the a.out kludge bit is what makes an ELF64 image loadable.

nodes.label: Remapping the 8259 before interrupts are enabled
nodes.source_location: The interrupt controller has to move
nodes.rationale: Out of reset IRQ 0-15 arrive as vectors 8-15, which are exceptions - a timer tick would report as a double fault, an accurate description of something that never happened.

nodes.label: x86-64 paging: four levels and accumulating permissions
nodes.rationale: The bottom three levels are ARM's L1/L2/L3 exactly and everything lives under 512 GB, so the extra level costs one page. Permissions accumulate down the walk, so intermediate entries are permissive and the leaf carries the policy - any other arrangement stores one permission in four places that can disagree.

nodes.label: CR0.WP, without which a read-only mapping is decoration
nodes.rationale: Out of reset a ring 0 write to a page with RW clear succeeds; the permission is enforced against ring 3 only, and AArch64 has no counterpart. Found by narrowing .text, reading the entry back correct, and watching a deliberate store go through.

nodes.label: CR4.SMEP, and why SMAP is off
nodes.rationale: One NX bit covers both privilege levels where ARM has PXN and UXN, so SMEP buys the guarantee with a control register instead of a descriptor bit. SMAP is deliberately off because the kernel reads user memory on every IPC.

nodes.label: The x86-64 context switch
nodes.rationale: Seventy-two bytes against AArch64's 656, and the difference is System V rather than the processor: every XMM register is caller-saved, so a thread that called the switch has already spilled its floating point. One stack moves rather than two, and rip cannot be moved to, so the restore pushes it and returns.

nodes.label: The GDT, the TSS and ring 3
nodes.rationale: A privilege level on ARM is bits in PSTATE; here it is a property of a segment descriptor. The order is arithmetic rather than convention because syscall and sysretq derive CS and SS from IA32_STAR. gdt_init runs before mmu_init because the processor writes the accessed bit into a descriptor.

nodes.label: syscall does not switch the stack
nodes.rationale: For two instructions the kernel runs at ring 0 on a stack the process chose, which is why IA32_FMASK clears IF. The kernel stack comes out of the TSS, so there is one answer to which stack an entry lands on rather than two that can disagree.

nodes.label: Lazy FP save, on either machine
nodes.rationale: -mno-mmx -mno-sse -mno-sse2 are this architecture's -mgeneral-regs-only: the kernel may not touch a floating-point register at all, and a flag turns that from a promise into a compile error, so a kernel thread never faults because it never can. CR0.TS is the disarm and vector 7 the fault.

nodes.label: -mno-red-zone
nodes.rationale: The red zone is 128 bytes below rsp a leaf function may use without adjusting the stack pointer, and an interrupt handler pushes straight over it. Nothing notices until there are interrupts, which is the worst time to find out.

nodes.label: Endianness, which turned out to be free
nodes.rationale: Checked rather than assumed: every string.pack in the on-disk format carries an explicit <, the network stack's put16/get16 do explicit shifts, and IPC structs never cross architectures because both ends are processes on the same machine.

nodes.label: virtio.c, below the HAL
nodes.rationale: Four devices speak virtio-mmio and the handshake is identical while the rings are not, so the conversation is shared and the ring is not. It is not a HAL interface - no other board implements it - which is why it lives under the board.

nodes.label: Two devices that are the same device
nodes.source_location: Two devices that are the same device
nodes.rationale: Keyboard and tablet are both virtio-input, device id 18, indistinguishable in the register window; telling them apart means asking each what events it can produce, which costs a partial bring-up. The file is instance-based because two devices of a kind cannot share a ring.

nodes.label: The display size as a compile-time constant
nodes.rationale: There is no allocator, so the pixels are a static array in a NOLOAD section. Nothing above the HAL needs telling; changing it at runtime needs a capped buffer, a protocol for every holder of a geometry copy, and virtio-gpu first so there are two implementations to design against.

nodes.label: virtio-gpu
nodes.rationale: The target that earns the HAL a flush, and where a mode set is a command to the device rather than a write to a config blob.

nodes.label: ramfb
nodes.rationale: The guest owns the configuration, so width, height and stride written back through fw_cfg is a mode change. Designing the runtime interface against it alone would produce ramfb's shape with a general name.

nodes.label: QEMU virt aarch64, the development target
nodes.rationale: PL011, GIC and virtio: standard, documented, serial straight to the terminal. Which exception level you get depends on the options, so read CurrentEL rather than assuming; secondary cores start and must be parked.

nodes.label: The GIC version is not the default
nodes.rationale: -M virt gives a GICv2; Kosmos drives a GICv3, so gic-version=3 is on the QEMU line, and booting on a plain -M virt finds no redistributor and never receives an interrupt. The fastest way to settle it is to dump the device tree rather than to remember.

nodes.label: Raspberry Pi 1, the argument answered no
nodes.rationale: Kept rather than deleted because it was a good argument: GPIO 14/15 are UART directly, one core, canonical mailbox framebuffer, and ARMv6 would force arch/ and hal/ genuinely apart. Refused because it is 32-bit - a complete second arch/armv6/ on a 700 MHz core, for a system whose question is whether it can be fast - and because x86-64 surfaces the same assumptions from a better direction.

nodes.label: Raspberry Pi 5, the main target
nodes.rationale: More hostile to bare metal than the Pi 4. Traps: the pitch is not width*4, BGRA rather than RGBA, an uncached framebuffer, MMIO differing from the Pi 4's, an unverified GIC version, a changed mailbox interface, and four cores started at once.

nodes.label: The RP1 southbridge wall
nodes.rationale: Nearly all I/O hangs off RP1 over PCIe, so a character out of the header UART would need PCIe and an RP1 driver before printf. The way out is the 3-pin JST-SH debug connector, which goes straight to the BCM2712's UART.

nodes.label: AArch64's weak memory model
nodes.rationale: Far more aggressive than x86: orderings x86 forgives fail here once every thousand boots, and it is the most expensive class of bug in the project.

nodes.label: NVIDIA Jetson, a cheap port
nodes.rationale: Same ISA, so only hal/ changes and it is a week. Against it: NVIDIA's signed boot chain makes the iteration cycle much worse than copying a file to an SD card.

nodes.label: PowerPC G4, the port that teaches the most
nodes.rationale: Valuable because it is big-endian, which lands in one precise place - the Lua table serializer - and forces an explicit wire format. Open Firmware solves the console; the cost is an inverted hashed page table with no analogy to a radix tree.

nodes.label: The Mac Pro 2013, rejected
nodes.rationale: No serial output at all - the RP1 problem without the back door. x86-64 in general is a better learning target than ARM; the problem is that machine.

nodes.label: The rule for choosing a target
nodes.source_location: The rule for choosing a target
nodes.rationale: If you cannot get a character out over serial in the first two hours, it is not a target. Everything else can be solved with time; that cannot.

nodes.label: The recommended porting order
nodes.rationale: QEMU virt, Pi 1, Pi 5, Jetson, G4 - easiest to debug first. Each jump breaks a different assumption, and porting before the design is proven generalises over assumptions not yet known to be correct.

nodes.label: make KVM=1 x86
nodes.rationale: Runs on an x86-64 Linux host's own cores and needs -cpu host, the same trade make fast makes on ARM; it does nothing on an Apple Silicon Mac.
